prompt: Why are Schlenk techniques, used with a high vacuum line and a dry box, so important in organometallic chemistry?

choices.text: Many organometallic compounds are sensitive to air and moisture and need an anaerobic environment
Most organometallic compounds are gases at room temperature and must be condensed
choices.why: Most organometallic compounds are nonvolatile crystalline solids. Only a few, such as Ni(CO)4, exist as vapors.

choices.text: None of the purification methods of organic chemistry work for organometallic compounds
choices.why: Many methods of organic chemistry can be used. The special techniques are needed because of air and moisture sensitivity.

choices.text: They are needed so that NMR spectra can be recorded under ^1H-decoupled conditions
choices.why: Decoupling is a setting of the NMR experiment. Schlenk techniques protect air- and moisture-sensitive compounds during synthesis, isolation and storage.

explanation: Organometallic compounds are mostly nonvolatile crystalline solids, so many methods of organic chemistry work for them, but they are comparatively sensitive to aerial oxygen and moisture. Schlenk techniques, with special glassware, a high vacuum line and a dry box, let chemists synthesize, isolate and store them in an air- and moisture-free environment.

prompt: Where do metal hydride signals usually appear in a ^1H NMR spectrum, and why?

choices.text: Between 0 and −40 ppm, upfield of TMS, because the metal d electrons shield the hydride
Between 0 and +40 ppm, downfield of TMS, because the metal deshields the hydride
choices.why: Hydride signals appear upfield (to high field) of TMS, because of shielding by the metal d electrons.

choices.text: Between 0 and −40 ppm, with the upfield shift getting smaller as the d^{n} count rises
choices.why: The extent of the upfield shift increases with higher d^{n} configuration, since more d electrons shield the hydride.

choices.text: As far out as 290 ppm, because the hydride ligand makes the complex paramagnetic
choices.why: Shifts that large come from paramagnetic complexes such as (η^6-C6H6)2V. Metal hydride signals appear between 0 and −40 ppm.

explanation: Metal hydrides appear in a distinctive chemical shift range, 0 to −40 ppm, to high field of TMS. The upfield shift is attributed to shielding by the metal d electrons, and it grows with higher d^{n} configuration. Coupling constants such as J_(P–H), when a phosphorus nucleus is within coupling range, also help in analyzing these compounds.

prompt: An off-resonance ^1H-decoupled ^13C experiment gives ^1J_(C–H) ≈ 160 Hz for a carbon in an organometallic ligand. What hybridization does this indicate?

choices.text: sp^2
sp
choices.why: An sp carbon shows a much larger ^1J_(C–H), about 250 Hz.

choices.text: sp^3
choices.why: An sp^3 carbon shows a smaller ^1J_(C–H), about 125 Hz.

choices.text: It can't be told, because ^1J_(C–H) doesn't depend on hybridization
choices.why: ^1J_(C–H) correlates directly with the hybridization of the C–H bond, which is why it carries vital structural information.

explanation: ^1J_(C–H) coupling constants correlate directly with the hybridization of the C–H bond: about 250 Hz for an sp center, 160 Hz for sp^2 and 125 Hz for sp^3. A value near 160 Hz points to an sp^2 carbon.

prompt: In the ^13C NMR spectrum of a phosphine complex, a carbon shows a coupling of about 100 Hz to one phosphorus atom and about 10 Hz to another. What does this tell you?

choices.text: The carbon is trans to the first phosphorus and cis to the second
The carbon is cis to the first phosphorus and trans to the second
choices.why: This is reversed. The trans P–C coupling, about 100 Hz, is larger than the cis coupling, about 10 Hz.

choices.text: Both phosphorus atoms are cis to the carbon, since only cis couplings are observed
choices.why: Both cis and trans P–C couplings are observed, and the trans coupling (about 100 Hz) is the larger one.

choices.text: The carbon is trans to both phosphorus atoms, and the two couplings differ only because of phosphine bulk
choices.why: Coupling size here reflects geometry: about 100 Hz for trans and about 10 Hz for cis. The 10 Hz coupling marks a cis phosphorus.

explanation: As in ^1H NMR, phosphorus–carbon coupling is observed in ^13C NMR spectra, and the trans coupling (about 100 Hz) is larger than the cis coupling (about 10 Hz). So the 100 Hz coupling identifies the phosphorus trans to the carbon and the 10 Hz coupling a cis phosphorus.

prompt: Which IR band would you assign to the CO stretch of an organometallic carbonyl compound?

choices.text: An intense band at 1950 cm^−1
A weak band at 1950 cm^−1
choices.why: CO stretching bands of organometallic carbonyls are distinctly intense, not weak.

choices.text: An intense band at 2350 cm^−1
choices.why: That lies above the 2100–1700 cm^−1 range in which organometallic CO bands appear.

choices.text: An intense band at 1450 cm^−1
choices.why: That lies below the 2100–1700 cm^−1 range in which organometallic CO bands appear.

explanation: Organometallic compounds containing carbonyl groups are regularly studied by IR spectroscopy: their CO peaks appear between 2100 and 1700 cm^−1 as distinctly intense peaks. An intense band at 1950 cm^−1 fits that description.

prompt: Using ν = 1/(2πc) √(k/m_r), suppose the force constant k of a C–O bond falls to 0.81 times its original value while the reduced mass stays the same. What is the ratio of the new stretching frequency to the old one, to two decimal places?
explanation: ν is proportional to √(k/m_r), so with m_r unchanged, ν_new/ν_old = √0.81 = 0.90. A weaker bond (smaller k) vibrates at a lower frequency; a heavier reduced mass would also lower ν. Note that ν follows √k, not k itself.

prompt: Why is neutron diffraction often preferred over X-ray diffraction for studying metal hydride complexes?

choices.text: X-rays show hydrogens only as weak peaks beside the metal; neutrons detect them more accurately
Neutron diffraction doesn't need a single crystal, while X-ray diffraction does
choices.why: Both are single crystal diffraction methods. The difference is how well they detect hydrogen atoms.

choices.text: X-ray diffraction can't give a three-dimensional structure of the molecule
choices.why: X-ray diffraction does give a three-dimensional structure at the molecular level. Its weakness is detecting hydrogen.

choices.text: Hydrides scatter X-rays so strongly that they swamp the metal's peaks
choices.why: It is the reverse: hydrogen atoms give weak peaks, while the electron-rich metal atoms give intense ones.

explanation: Single crystal X-ray and neutron diffraction both give three-dimensional structures at the molecular level. X-ray diffraction, which rests on Bragg's law, is not sensitive enough to detect hydrogen atoms well: they appear as weak peaks beside the intense peaks of the electron-rich metal atoms. Neutron diffraction detects hydrogens more accurately, so it is good for analyzing metal hydride complexes.
